title.en: Boundary conditions are part of the physics

summary: Choose and display the boundary condition, because the same equation gives different answers at different edges.
objective: Make a field simulation state what happens at its edges rather than leaving it implicit.
applies_when: A source-free heat conduction field is simulated on a bounded domain, or another field equation is used and its own boundary conditions and conserved quantities have been stated.
The scene shows a rod, plate, container or region with edges.
Steady state or long-time behaviour is discussed.
intent_signals: why does it settle to zero
example_prompts: Simulate heat along a rod with the ends held at fixed temperature.
Let me switch the ends between held and insulated.
negative_signals: Unbounded analytic solutions where no domain edge exists.
Purely decorative field animations that make no physical claim.
not_for: Unbounded analytic solutions where no domain edge exists.
Purely decorative field animations that make no physical claim.

principles: The equation alone does not determine the solution. Holding the ends at a fixed temperature and insulating them are different physical situations with different long-time behaviour, even with identical initial conditions.

In the heat equation, fixed-value ends correspond to contact with a reservoir at that temperature, while an insulated end is expressed by a zero gradient there, meaning no heat flows across the boundary.
Higher modes decay fastest, so after a while the solution resembles its slowest surviving component; which component that is depends on the boundary condition.
Because the boundary is where the physics enters, it deserves visible treatment in the scene rather than being an unlabelled edge of a mesh.
implementation: Choose the boundary condition explicitly and show it in the scene, for example as a clamp, a reservoir or an insulating jacket.

Implement the condition consistently with the stencil and the time level you are updating. Assigning fixed boundary values after an interior update is a valid implementation when the interior update did not depend on stale boundary values; what matters is that the discrete boundary condition holds for the state you then display.
Let the viewer switch conditions and observe the different long-time behaviour, which is the clearest demonstration of why they matter.
State the initial condition alongside the boundary condition, since the transient depends on both.
Label the quantity and units on the display, and report the steady state the current conditions imply.
observable_checks: Run to long times with fixed ends and confirm the interior approaches the steady solution those ends imply: a uniform value only when both ends are held at the same value, and a linear profile between them when they differ.
Run with insulated ends and no internal sources or sinks, and confirm the appropriately weighted total thermal energy stays constant within tolerance rather than decaying.
Switch conditions mid-run and confirm the subsequent behaviour changes accordingly.

Check the discrete boundary residual at an insulated end: the one-sided difference should be zero to within the default tolerance rule (knowledge.validation-default-tolerance-rule) unless this record states its own, since a finite-difference implementation will not produce an exact analytic zero.

creative_affordances: Physical staging of the boundary, such as visible ice baths or insulation, makes the model legible and is a free design choice.
Comparative side-by-side runs with different conditions are often the strongest presentation.
known_limits: Authored modelling guidance citing one-dimensional heat-equation boundary conditions; other equations have their own boundary types.
No simulation has been run and no numerical accuracy is asserted.

claims.statement: For the one-dimensional heat equation, ends held at a fixed temperature represent contact with a reservoir at that temperature, insulated ends are expressed by a zero spatial derivative at the boundary meaning no heat flows there, and in the series solution the higher modes decay fastest so the long-time behaviour is dominated by the slowest surviving term.
claims.scope: One-dimensional linear heat conduction with constant coefficients; other equations and geometries require their own treatment.
